comments.author: @MistyRainne
comments.text:
Driving from the Willamette Valley to the coast goes through a lot of forests with roads cut through them. It's like driving through a canyon. Beautiful in its own way even before reaching the coast itself. (But the coast is the sort of place you wear a jacket to even in summer.)

I dunno why it's relatively non-religious. We're not the only place in the world with mountains and forests. If anything I would think it'd make people _more_ religious to see the world in all its glory. But like most places in the world, most of the population are city folk.

As for the volcanoes, we're part of the Pacific Ring Of Fire; so we have that connection too with Japan and other places along the Pacific. The Juan de Fuca Plate is a remnant of the once-vast Farallon Plate being subducted under the Americas (there are some other remnants down in Central/South America). It's probably where the Rocky Mountains came from, and California's geography largely comes from scraping off various stuff from former lands that have since been subducted.

In general, I like it here. It's a nice place that gets overlooked a lot, so all the flies that get drawn to popularity go elsewhere.

comments.text:
Great video, Geoff! As a born-and-raised Oregonian, here are a few deep-cut local nuggets to go with the "54°40' or Fight!" segment:

 It's really "ore-GONE": Locals love correcting out-of-staters, but the name traces back to the Ouragon River—from the French ouragan ("hurricane") for those brutal Columbia Gorge winds.

 A dead trapper built our government: In 1841, settlers only formed a provisional government because wealthy trapper Ewing Young died without a will and they needed a probate court to divvy up his estate.

 French Prairie was here first: Before the wagon trains, a tiny group of French-Canadian trappers held down the valley, spoke French to the U.S. envoy, and nearly voted down an American government at Champoeg in 1843.

replies.author: @EmbraceComplexityNow
replies.text: @nikkininedoor1480 At the time described, Canada did not exist as a country. The area Geoff described was designated by an 1818 treaty and jointly controlled by Britain and the US. Britain called it the “Columbia District” and the US called it “Oregon Country.” The treaty of 1846 established the boundary between British land and the US, and the US portion was called the “Oregon Territory” shortly thereafter. “British Columbia” was formed as a British Colony in 1858. Later, in 1867,  British colonies in North America were consolidated as Canada. So at the time Geoff described, the province of British Columbia did not exist.

16:11 -- Mount Shasta isn't the end of Cascadia. Mount Lassen is the southernmost volcanic peak in the range.
